name: Battle of the Pyramids
info: On 21 July 1798 Bonaparte's French army, formed in squares, defeated Murad Bey's Mamluk-led force near Embabeh in Ottoman Egypt, shattering Murad's field army and opening the way to Cairo.

facts.place: Near the village of Embabeh on the left bank of the Nile, in sight of the Pyramids of Giza, Ottoman Egypt (present-day Egypt)
facts.sides: The French army under General Bonaparte, in five divisions under Desaix, Reynier, Dugua, Vial and Bon; the Mamluk-led forces of Murad Bey, with elite armoured cavalry and fellahin militia, while Ibrahim Bey's army watched from across the Nile
facts.outcome: The French took the fortified village of Embabeh and broke Murad Bey's army, which retreated to Upper Egypt. French losses were reported at about 300; Mamluk and Ottoman casualties are estimated from several thousand to as many as 10,000.

t: The French formed each of five divisions into hollow rectangles, with cavalry and baggage in the centre and cannon at the corners, and these squares withstood repeated cavalry charges.
Murad Bey's plan was to hold the French on his fortified flanks, at Embabeh and Biktil, and strike their centre with cavalry, but Bon's division stormed Embabeh near the river.

The victory opened the way to Cairo and marked the beginning of the end of seven centuries of Mamluk dominance, but its strategic effect was short-lived once Nelson destroyed the French fleet ten days later.
dyk: Bonaparte named the battle after the Pyramids, although the Great Pyramid of Giza was distant from the field. In his order of the day he told his men that from the top of those pyramids forty centuries were contemplating them.
ev: The French under General Bonaparte capture Alexandria on 2 July and march across the desert toward Cairo
On 13 July French artillery wins the skirmish at Shubra Khit and destroys the Mamluk flagship on the Nile
On 21 July the French squares repel the Mamluk cavalry and Bon's division storms Embabeh
Bonaparte enters Cairo on 24 July and sets up a French administration
Ten days after the battle Nelson's fleet defeats the French navy at the Battle of the Nile
On 11 August French forces catch up with Ibrahim Bey and defeat him at Salalieh
Desaix defeats Murad Bey in Upper Egypt in the late months of the year

sections.background:
French forces landed in Ottoman-controlled Egypt and captured Alexandria on 2 July 1798. The army under General Bonaparte then marched across the desert toward Cairo. Its objective was to break the power of the Mamluk beys who dominated Egypt and to secure control of the capital before Ottoman reinforcements could arrive.

Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey, two Georgian Mamluks, commanded the country's military forces and prepared to oppose the advance. Their army included elite, heavily armoured cavalry, supported by fellahin militia serving as infantry. The French encountered the Mamluks about 9 miles (14 kilometres) from the Pyramids and 4 miles (6.4 kilometres) from Cairo.

On 13 July French scouts located Murad's encampment near Shubra Khit, and Bonaparte ordered an immediate advance. The skirmish that followed, at Shubra Khit, which is also called Chobrakit, saw French artillery destroy the Mamluk flagship on the Nile and force a retreat. It gave Bonaparte his first victory in Egypt after the landing and showed the effectiveness of concentrated firepower against cavalry charges.
sections.forces:
The French army was organised into five divisions. Each was formed into a hollow rectangle with the cavalry and baggage in the centre and cannon at the corners. From right to left the divisions were commanded by Louis Desaix, Jean-Louis-Ébénézer Reynier, Charles-François-Joseph Dugua, Honoré Vial and Louis André Bon. Desaix also sent a detachment to occupy the nearby village of Biktil. Before the fighting Bonaparte exhorted his men to remain steady when facing the Mamluk cavalry, telling them that they had come to save the inhabitants from barbarism and that from the top of the pyramids forty centuries were contemplating them.

The French advanced south in echelon, with the right flank leading and the left secured by the Nile. Murad Bey anchored his right on the Nile at Embabeh, which was fortified with infantry and artillery, and his left on Biktil, where he placed additional guns. His Mamluk cavalry deployed in the centre. Across the Nile, the army of Ibrahim Bey watched the battle but was unable to cross and intervene.

Murad's plan was to hold the French on his fortified flanks and then strike their centre with cavalry. The Mamluk force combined heavily armoured horsemen with militia infantry and artillery in fixed positions, while the French relied on disciplined squares with muskets and guns.
sections.course:
On 21 July, after marching all night, the French reached the vicinity of the village of Embabeh. After a short rest Bonaparte ordered his troops to form for battle, and they advanced in their squares. Repeated cavalry charges were directed against the French squares. One armoured rider advanced to within a few steps of the French lines and demanded a duel, but was shot down by musket fire.

At about 15:30 Murad ordered his defterdar, Ayyub Bey, to lead a mass assault. The divisions of Desaix, Reynier and Dugua held firm, repelling the horsemen with musketry and artillery. Some of the Mamluks then attempted to attack Desaix's detached force, but without success. The Egyptian chronicler al-Jabarti described the fight as lasting about three-quarters of an hour, with drums, gunfire and so much dust and smoke that the sky darkened and people thought the earth had moved.

Near the river, Bon's division deployed into attack columns and stormed Embabeh. The garrison broke, and many fled into the Nile, where hundreds drowned. Murad himself was wounded in the cheek by a sabre but escaped with several thousand cavalry to Upper Egypt.
sections.aftermath:
French reports listed 29 killed and 260 wounded, and French losses were reported at about 300 in all. Murad's losses were far heavier, with thousands killed or wounded, including Ayyub Bey and perhaps 3,000 of the elite Mamluk cavalry. Estimates of Mamluk and Ottoman casualties vary widely, from several thousand to as many as 10,000.

Upon hearing news of the defeat of their cavalry, the Mamluk armies waiting in Cairo dispersed to Syria. Bonaparte entered the capital on 24 July. On 11 August French forces caught up with Ibrahim Bey and inflicted a defeat on him at Salalieh. Murad, in Upper Egypt, waged a guerrilla campaign until Desaix defeated him in late 1799.

In Cairo, Bonaparte instituted French administration and suppressed later rebellions with force. He tried to co-opt the local ulama, but scholars such as al-Jabarti poured scorn on the cultural claims of the French. Ten days after the battle, Admiral Horatio Nelson destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile, which cut Bonaparte's army off from France and curtailed his ambitions in the region.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from French reports, which list 29 killed and 260 wounded on the French side, and from the Egyptian chronicler al-Jabarti, whose History of Egypt describes the Mamluks being defeated at the gates of Cairo. Bonaparte's own order of the day, with its reference to forty centuries, survives as well.

Casualty figures are uncertain. French losses are put at about 300, but estimates of Mamluk and Ottoman casualties run from several thousand to as many as 10,000. The figure of perhaps 3,000 elite Mamluk cavalry killed or wounded is likewise an estimate.
sections.legacy:
The battle signalled the beginning of the end of seven centuries of Mamluk dominance in Egypt. Its strategic effect was short-lived, since ten days later Nelson destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile and the army was cut off from France. Abdullah al-Sharqawi, who headed Bonaparte's Cairo divan, later described the occupiers as materialist, libertine philosophers who deny the resurrection, the afterlife and the prophets, while the mathematician Joseph Fourier lamented that the Muslim religion would on no account permit the development of the mind.

The battle has been a frequent subject in art. François-André Vincent made a preparatory sketch and a painting of it, and later artists include Antoine-Jean Gros, Carle Vernet and François-Louis-Joseph Watteau. In popular culture it appears in Ridley Scott's 2023 film Napoleon, whose depiction has been criticised for historical inaccuracies, such as showing French troops firing on the pyramids.

summary: On 21 July 1798 Bonaparte's French army, formed in squares, repelled Murad Bey's Mamluk cavalry near Embabeh and stormed the fortified village, breaking Murad's army and opening the way to Cairo. The victory was blunted ten days later at the Battle of the Nile.

notes: The article gives no strengths for either army; I give none, and say only what it says of their make-up.
Sections are shorter than 1,100 characters in places because the article is short; I did not pad with outside facts.
The article says French losses 'about 300' (lead) and '29 killed and 260 wounded' (body); both are given.
The Nile battle is dated only as 'ten days later'; the ev entry uses that wording and sits before Salalieh (11 August) on that reckoning.
'Late 1799' for Murad's defeat by Desaix is the article's phrase; the ev label is the year 1799.
The article's quotation from al-Jabarti is paraphrased, not quoted. The article's 'legendary cavalry' and 'crushing defeat' are not used.
The one-line 'first victory' at Shubra Khit is as the article states; 'in Egypt after the landing' is my gloss and may be trimmed.
